title: Original Jurassic Park and the computers

commenti.body:
It comes through to some extent in the film, but I think the issue, especially when it comes to sequels, is that if you have a computer next to a giant dinosaur, I know which one I'm gonna wanna focus on.

It's an interesting thought though, having not read the book, I never really thought about all the technological failures in the film, especially given that it came out just as PCs were becoming commonplace

I agree with you. I'm not sure why they decided to take the focus away from that. Perhaps they thought it had been explored in the first movie and they would not have anything new to add. Or maybe they didn't even see the potential there for the drama to be not just about man vs. dinosaurs but also machine. It wouldn't be surprising if Hollywood missed that, as they have a tendency to go for the lowest common denominator type stuff. So scary looking beasts

I like this take, never thought about it this way. Leaving the book aside (never read it, sadly), I always saw it as the perils of humans relying too much on technology - not technology as a villain itself, as in HAL 9000. I saw it as computers and other man-made inventions giving the characters the false hope they were protected, and it ends up biting them in the ass (just as bringing dinosaurs back to life without a second thought to the overall implications, a sign of human arrogance).

What I truly miss about the original is the sense of wonder, how this characters get a chance to marvel at those extraordinary creatures before it ventures into monster movie territory. The other ones treat the dinosaurs as common figures in this new reality. The stories are mostly about financial greed, plain and simple.

The book is such a different story with significantly different characters that it’s well worth a read even if you know the film back to front.

Perfect as the movie is, it’d be super interesting to see a more faithful adaptation of the book as a mini-series some day.

To me a important aspect of the story is you can not really get mad at the dinosaurs, they are just doing what comes naturally, the real 'monsters' of the movies are the humans, also doing what comes naturally, and in that regard, it is arrogance, greed, stupidity etc.

The lawyer just wants to make money, Hammond just wants to put on a show etc it is not until people like Ellie point out the plants are poisonous and Grant highlights the 'T-Rex does want to be fed' etc is there any consideration by anyone capable of bringing them back into the world as actually living breathing things and not just exhibits etc.

So there is, to me, at least not 'relying on technology' but not actually respected the power that technology and advancement brings, and therefore the weight of responsibility it should be wielded with. Malcolm says as much in his rant at the dinner table.

I think the follow up movies have the standard issue almost all sequels have, film makers that fail to grasp what the point of the original story was. Even when the same people are involved, as was the case with TLW it did not nearly have the time to bake to fully realize the issues at hand, and does not want to tread the same ground. Even just the aspect of wonder at the dinosaurs before it all goes wrong runs the risk of feeling like the movie is just treading water until the action starts which Jurassic World felt like to me. It is hard to have that same sense when the audience knows what to expect, and what is going to happen, and in the case of the movies, the characters know the events of the previous movie. Only something like Aliens where most of the characters discount the reality the audience knows to expect does that same sense of sudden panic can actually happen when what we all know is going to happen, happens.

An important theme in the book, is the issue of increasing technological complexity. Hammond and his scientists are extremely proud of their cloning work, but they fail to understand the complexities of life that form the foundation of what they do. Just as much as they fail to understand the complexity of the park's security system, and its foundation. There's a paralel there. Ian Malcolm tries to convey how chaos develops in complex systems, and how the more complex the system, the more unpredictable the outcome.

Certainly in using the term “monsters”, I understand all monsters are relative anyway. Often we make our own monsters which is definitely a theme in the story. Basically the technology is an obstacle, kind of its own beast that is out of control.

It might have been partially a product of the time. People were becoming interested in computers and what role they play in our world. In some ways it probably wouldn’t have the same impact now, though I still love movies where technology poses a problem that has to be solved.

Technology has ended up as a “character” in a lot of iconic stories. Was the millennium Falcon for example not a kind of dynamic living part of Star Wars that attracted people to the story?
It certainly does come through in the first film, though sometimes in a weird kind of unexplained way. For example the line of dialogue “whiterabbit.obj” which wouldn’t make much sense to any viewer.
